Zovereign Source

Self-hosted Zcash infrastructure · one Docker image

Run your own Zcash stack.

Zovereign lets you run lightwalletd and a Zcash archive full node with one command. Connect your wallets to your own infrastructure, transact without a third-party RPC provider, and build privacy-focused apps.

Get started

No registry login, separate RPC provider, Docker-in-Docker or RPC credentials. Pick one way to run it. Both create the same zovereign container and zovereign-data volume.

Published image · nothing to clone

shell
docker run -d --platform linux/amd64 \
  --name zovereign --restart unless-stopped --stop-timeout 120 \
  --log-driver json-file --log-opt max-size=20m --log-opt max-file=3 \
  --mount type=volume,src=zovereign-data,dst=/data \
  -p 8233:8233 -p 127.0.0.1:9067:9067 \
  ghcr.io/zcashlabs/zovereign:latest
  • --mount …zovereign-data keeps databases and download progress across container replacement.
  • 127.0.0.1:9067 publishes wallet gRPC to your machine only.
  • --stop-timeout 120 gives both databases time to flush on stop.

From source · build locally with Compose

shell
git clone https://github.com/zcashlabs/zovereign.git
cd zovereign
docker compose up -d --build
  • Same defaults: bounded logs, two-minute shutdown grace, loopback gRPC, persistent volume.
  • Optional: copy .env.example to .env to change ports, download concurrency or disk reserve.
  • Pause with docker compose stop; resume with docker compose start.

  1. Check logs

    Follow the download and startup progress.

    logs
    docker logs -f --tail=100 zovereign
    →

  2. Wait for healthy

    Check until the status changes from starting to healthy.

    health
    docker inspect --format '{{.State.Health.Status}}' zovereign
    →

  3. Connect your wallet

    Once healthy, set your wallet’s custom server to:

    127.0.0.1:9067

    Use a wallet that supports plaintext connections. For remote access, use a trusted tunnel or configure TLS.

Keep the volume. Stop gracefully with docker stop -t 120 zovereign. Removing or replacing the container keeps zovereign-data; deleting the volume means downloading ~300 GB again.

Performance

Mainnet startup on 14 November 2026, using a Linux amd64 VPS with 12 CPU threads, 32 GiB RAM and a 1 TB SSD.

First startup
≈99 min
Zakura snapshot download
≈275 GB
lightwalletd snapshot download
≈24.6 GB

Startup breakdown

  • Download, verify & restore: ≈86 min
  • Other setup and interruptions
  • Zakura catch-up: ≈40 sec

One development run, including interruptions and fixes. Times vary with bandwidth, disk speed and snapshot age. No from-scratch comparison was measured.

Bring a real machine.

This is an archive node, not a toy. First boot moves about 300 GB compressed (≈275 GB Zakura + ≈25 GB lightwalletd), then verifies and extracts it, so plan the disk accordingly.

On a fast SSD host with good bandwidth, expect the first end-to-end install to take roughly 2–3 hours. Slower links and disks take longer. Later starts reuse the data.

  • Linux amd64 — tested platform.
  • Docker Desktop / WSL 2 — allocate these resources to Docker’s VM, not just the host.
  • Native ARM64 — not supported.
  • Apple Silicon — runs under amd64 emulation; a full mainnet restore has not passed validation there.

Inside the container

One process tree, two daemons, one volume, three ports, and a clear opinion about which of them the internet gets to see.

  1. 1

    Supervisor

    Tini handles PID 1 while a Python supervisor downloads, verifies, restores, drops privileges, and runs both daemons as a pair: if either exits, its peer is stopped and Docker restarts the whole stack.

  2. 2

    Zakura archive node

    Full mainnet history in archive mode, restored from a snapshot instead of rebuilt from the network, then kept current from peers.

  3. 3

    Private RPC

    Node RPC listens on 127.0.0.1:8232 inside the container. It is never published to the host. No credentials to generate, rotate or leak.

  4. 4

    lightwalletd

    Starts with a populated compact-block cache and catches up from your node. The health probe makes it serve a real block before Docker calls the stack healthy.

  5. 5

    One named volume

    zovereign-data holds both databases and any unfinished downloads. It outlives the container, so updates mean replace the box, keep the data.

  6. 6

    Peer port 8233

    The one port meant for the internet: the node’s connection to other Zcash peers.

  7. 7

    Wallet port 9067

    lightwalletd gRPC, bound to your host’s loopback by default. Serving another machine is a deliberate choice: an SSH tunnel, a private network, or your own TLS certificate.

Questions people actually ask.

How long does the first start take?

Hours, not minutes. It has to download roughly 300 GB, hash all of it, extract it, then let Zakura catch up past the snapshot. On a fast SSD host with good bandwidth we estimate 2–3 hours end to end; our own development run took about 99 minutes including interruptions. Slower disks or links take longer, and we don’t promise a fixed time.

And every start after that?

Much shorter. A completed bootstrap is reused without contacting the snapshot publishers, so a restart is just the two daemons starting on existing databases and catching up on whatever happened while they were stopped.

What if my download gets interrupted?

Start the container again. Completed ranges persist in a .part file and the chosen snapshot is pinned, so it resumes the same archive rather than starting over, even if a newer snapshot has been published in the meantime.

Do I need a separate full node, RPC provider or credentials?

No. Zakura is bundled, its RPC listens on loopback inside the container, and lightwalletd connects to it there. There is no Docker socket, no registry login and no credentials file to manage.

Can my phone wallet use it from elsewhere?

Not by default, deliberately. gRPC binds to your host’s loopback. To serve another machine, use an SSH tunnel or a private network, or mount a certificate and key and set TLS_CERT / TLS_KEY. The deployment guide shows the exact command.

What happens if one of the daemons crashes?

They live and die as a pair. If either exits, the supervisor stops its peer gracefully and exits, and Docker’s restart policy brings the whole stack back on the same volume.

Will it run on my M-series Mac?

It runs under amd64 emulation, but a full mainnet restore under emulation has not passed validation, and native ARM64 isn’t supported. Linux amd64 is the tested platform. On any Docker Desktop, allocate the CPU, memory and disk to Docker’s VM.

How do I update without losing anything?

Pull the new image, stop with a 120-second grace period, remove the container, and run the same command again with the same zovereign-data volume. The databases stay put. Check release notes first: an incompatible database is refused, not silently replaced. Pin a sha-<commit> tag or digest when you want controlled upgrades.

Is this trustless?

No. Checksums protect integrity, not authenticity, and imported history depends on the snapshot publishers. What you do get is your own node and wallet server, with no third-party RPC in the path from here on. See the deployment guide.

Own the endpoint your wallet talks to.

One image. One volume. One command. The rest is your node’s business.
